parts.label: c
parts.display_text: A missile is launched from a rocket moving at +0.80c relative to Earth. Its velocity relative to the rocket is −0.62c. Calculate the velocity of the missile relative to Earth. (The source mistakenly asks for the rocket velocity.)

duplicate-dfcb6efdf3c445ce.hint: At speeds comparable with c, ordinary addition of velocities is no longer valid.
notes: For collinear motion, u′ = (u − v)/(1 − uv/c²), with signed velocities. Use the inverse relation for the opposite transformation.
Check the low-speed limit and that a light signal still has speed c. A result exceeding c for a material object indicates a sign or formula error.

duplicate-1d6e42a1e420a75e.hint: Compare the velocity direction with the magnetic-field direction. Only the perpendicular component is deflected.
notes: The magnetic force is |F| = |q|vB sin θ. For perpendicular circular motion, |q|vB = mv²/r, giving r = mv/(|q|B).
A magnetic field alone does no work: the force is perpendicular to velocity. Reverse the force direction for a negative charge.

notes: At non-relativistic speeds, v(A relative to C) = v(A relative to B) + v(B relative to C). Resolve perpendicular directions separately.
For a magnitude and direction, combine the components using Pythagoras and a labelled angle. Do not add the magnitudes of perpendicular velocities.

duplicate-42cfda8b40dede5c.hint: Which observer measures the object at rest? That observer measures its proper length.
notes: For length parallel to the relative motion, L = L₀/γ. L₀ is the rest length; perpendicular dimensions are unchanged.
Measuring length in a frame requires positions of both ends at the same time in that frame. Do not combine one frame’s distance with another frame’s time.

ibd-11a79c754c11e170-q4:whole.text: Maxwell’s theory identifies light as an electromagnetic wave with a definite propagation speed in vacuum. Special relativity takes this vacuum speed c to be the same for every inertial observer, independently of the motion of the source. The electromagnetic laws therefore have the same form in all inertial frames.

ibd-a570e27c0010b5b2-q4:whole.text: The journey takes 2000/(0.98 × 3.0 × 10⁸) ≈ 6.8 μs in the ground frame. Without time dilation this is about three mean lifetimes, so only a small fraction would survive. Time dilation increases the mean lifetime in this frame to γτ₀ = 5.0 × 2.2 = 11 μs, allowing a much larger fraction to reach the ground. The observed number of muons supports the dilated lifetime; a mean lifetime is not a fixed expiry time for every particle.

fep-3fb598f3b26e81bc-qD1:whole.text: Yes: the two arrivals at Hermann occur at the same place and at the same time, so they are a single coincident event. Here Δx = 0 and Δt = 0; a Lorentz transformation gives Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²) = 0. This does not establish that the two spatially separated emissions were simultaneous in every frame.

fep-f1e4db817c42d843-qD1:whole.text: Yes: the two arrivals at Hermann occur at the same place and at the same time, so they are a single coincident event. fep-0401f909c25295c4-qG1:whole.text: The landings are not simultaneous in Simon’s frame. In the ground frame Simon moves towards the light from the front end and away from the light from the rear end. In Simon’s frame light still travels at c and the midpoint is equally far from the two ends; the earlier arrival from the front therefore corresponds to an earlier landing at the end towards which the carriage moves.

fep-49b3d1fd7578318d-qG2:whole.text: Nino does not see the two hits as simultaneous. In the ground frame the train moves to the right: L moves towards the left-going pulse while R moves away from the right-going pulse. Both pulses travel at c in that frame, so the pulse reaches L first. Clare, at rest at the train’s midpoint, measures equal travel times to the two ends.
